section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department correspondence, diplomatic despatches, telegrams, and analytical memoranda from February to May 1932 detailing the dual external and internal crises confronting Japan. It traces the fallout of military actions in Shanghai and Manchuria, the 61st extraordinary session of the Imperial Diet, and the Seiyukai party's landslide election victory amidst severe economic depression. A central focus is the sharp rise of ultra-nationalist terrorism and reactionary societies, highlighted by the Blood Brotherhood (Ketsumeidan) assassinations of Baron Takuma Dan and Junnosuke Inouye, military insubordination, and an exhaustive Embassy catalogue of over a hundred right-wing organizations.

subfiles.about: Continuation of a confidential letter discussing diplomatic exchanges in Tokyo with Japanese leaders regarding troop deployments to Shanghai and domestic political crosscurrents.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports on joint conferences with British and French diplomats and Japanese Foreign Minister Yoshizawa regarding the dispatch of 12,000 to 18,000 Japanese troops to Shanghai. He describes conversations with Admiral Toyoda and special envoy Yosuke Matsuoka, reiterating that the United States would take no position hostile to China while urging Japan to allow Chinese negotiators to save face. Forbes also addresses rumors propagated by Foreign Office spokesman Toshio Shiratori misrepresenting Forbes's remarks about Japan's military actions in Manchuria and Shanghai.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Forbes to Secretary of State Stimson regarding the Shanghai Crisis and Political Tensions (Continuation)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a memorandum regarding the French Ambassador's assessment of Japanese vulnerabilities.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Stimson memo recording the French Ambassador's view that Japan's weaknesses would eventually cause its failure.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/370 regarding French Ambassador's Views on Japanese Weakness

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a report on the lessening likelihood of a coup d'état by young army officers.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Forbes's 1932 communication assessing a diminishing threat of coup d'état from younger Japanese army officers.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/371 regarding Diminishing Danger of Military Coup d'État

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a telegram reporting rumors of impending cabinet changes following the Diet session.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Forbes's 1932 telegram on Tokyo rumors of major Cabinet reorganization after the Diet's adjournment.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/372 regarding Rumors of Cabinet Reorganization

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting on the easing of international tensions over Shanghai, domestic political instability, and the extraordinary Diet session.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports eased tension after Japan's announced Shanghai withdrawal, though Manchurian banditry continues; the Home Minister resigned, leaving Inukai dual portfolios amid reorganization rumors, with an emergency ¥83 million military budget pending Diet approval.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 101 from Ambassador Forbes regarding Easing International Tension and Domestic Political Maneuvering
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Telegram transmitting a news report from Shanghai regarding fears of a fascist uprising in Japan and General Shirakawa's farewell message to returning troops.
subfiles.from: Mahlon Fay Perkins, American Chargé d'Affaires in Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram relays a Reuter report that the Seiyukai government is failing Japan's crisis, prompting maneuvers for a national or military government to forestall fascism; General Shirakawa's farewell address warned troops to stay ready.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 359 from Peiping Legation Transmitting Reuter Report on Japanese Political Crisis and General Shirakawa's Address
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a telegram concerning Japanese civilian administration difficulties due to military uncommunicativeness.
subfiles.from: Mahlon Fay Perkins, American Chargé d'Affaires in Peiping
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram: Japan's government faced administrative trouble because military authorities withheld reports exceeding official instructions.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/374 regarding Japanese Administrative Difficulties with the Military

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential telegram relaying views of a high-ranking Japanese official traveling in China on Manchuria, the League of Nations, and military insubordination.
subfiles.from: Mahlon Fay Perkins, American Chargé d'Affaires in Peiping
subfiles.summary: A Japanese investigator's relayed views: Japan won't annex Manchuria but insists on cooperative local administration, might quit the League, wants to exit Shanghai gracefully, seeks Kuomintang's replacement while engaging Chiang, and notes Tokyo's embarrassment over unreported military actions.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 350 from Peiping Legation Relaying Japanese Official's Views on Manchuria, China, and Military Autonomy
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Detailed confidential letter describing the assassination of Baron Dan, threats against moderate leaders and the press, police crackdowns on a right-wing assassination league, and embassy policy.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes recounts the fatal shooting on March 5 of Mitsui director Baron Takuma Dan by a young nationalist assassin using a weapon linked to the murderer of Junnosuke Inouye. He details the existence of an ultra-nationalist death band targeting moderate figures including Shidehara, Makino, and Wakatsuki, as well as police alerts regarding threats against The Japan Advertiser and Dr. Inazo Nitobe's intimidation by military officers. Forbes also covers Prince Saionji's consultations aimed at curbing military extremism, ultra-nationalist newspaper attacks against American diplomacy, and a unanimous embassy staff consensus that continuing aggressive foreign diplomatic protests would push Japan straight into war.
subfiles.title: Confidential Letter from Ambassador Forbes to Secretary of State Stimson on the Assassination of Baron Dan and the Rise of Political Terrorism
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a telegram concerning General McCoy's conclusion that the Manchurian campaign was planned independently by the military.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, U.S. Minister to China
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram: General McCoy found the Manchurian operation premeditated by the military without Shidehara's or the Premier's knowledge.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/376 regarding General McCoy's Findings on Military Premeditation in Manchuria

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram reporting General McCoy's briefing on the Lytton Commission's itinerary and observations on military control in Shanghai.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, U.S. Minister to China
subfiles.summary: Johnson relays McCoy's League Commission itinerary through Nanking/Hankow/Peiping/Manchuria/Korea/Japan, his conviction the occupation was purely military-planned, and Johnson's own view that Japanese military dominated Shanghai peace talks over diplomat Shigemitsu.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Minister Johnson Reporting on League Commission Schedule and Japanese Military Dominance
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing periodic political report No. 51 on the February 1932 Japanese general election.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Forbes's despatch indexing the Seiyukai's decisive general-election victory.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/377 regarding Results of the Japanese General Election

subfiles.about: Political report section analyzing the Seiyukai's sweeping victory in the February 1932 general elections and the Minseito's defeat.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (W. Cameron Forbes)
subfiles.summary: Report details Japan's February 1932 election: Seiyukai's 304-147 landslide over Minseito, attributed to relief promises against depression versus Minseito's unpopular retrenchment and leadership disarray after Inouye's assassination.
subfiles.title: Report Excerpt from Tokyo Embassy on the Japanese General Election of February 20, 1932

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a State Department memorandum on feudal political structures and military clan dominance in Japan.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Hornbeck memo on persistent feudal structures and military clan aristocracy dominating Japanese politics.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/379 regarding Feudal Conditions and Military Clan Aristocracy in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 11 from Taihoku concerning administrative reorganizations in colonial Taiwan.
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Ketcham's 1932 Taihoku despatch indexing personnel changes in the Taiwan Government General.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/380 regarding Personnel Changes in the Taiwan Government General

subfiles.about: Consular despatch reporting high-level political and military personnel changes in colonial Taiwan following the installation of the Inukai Cabinet.
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.summary: Ketcham reports Governor Ota's resignation and Minami's succession (tied to Prince Saionji), Kinoshita's replacement by Yakata stressing South China/Philippines/Malaysia trade links, Masaki's promotion and replacement by Abe, and strict military censorship of civilian administrators.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 11 from Consulate Taihoku on Personnel Reorganization in the Taiwan Government General
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 538 reporting on the extraordinary session of the Imperial Diet convened for emergency military appropriations.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Neville's 1932 despatch on the 61st Diet session approving emergency funding for China operations.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/381 regarding the Sixty-First Session of the Imperial Diet

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting a review of the extraordinary Diet session along with formal addresses delivered by Foreign Minister Yoshizawa and War Minister Araki.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville describes the extraordinary session of the Diet held March 18-24, 1932, which was forced by the Privy Council's refusal to approve full emergency funding for military operations in Shanghai and Manchuria through Imperial ordinances alone. Enclosure 1 provides Foreign Minister Yoshizawa's speech defending Japanese actions during the Shanghai incident, protesting League of Nations interference under Article 15, acknowledging Manchukuo's declaration of independence, and discussing Soviet fisheries negotiations. Enclosure 2 transmits War Minister Sadao Araki's speech reviewing military operations in Manchuria and Shanghai, praising army-navy coordination, and demanding wholehearted national support for the armed forces.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 538 from Tokyo Reporting on the 61st Extraordinary Diet Session, with Speeches by Yoshizawa and Araki
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic report on right-wing terrorism, police investigations of the Blood Brotherhood assassination network, and political unrest in Japan.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Neville examines the wave of reactionism following the murders of Baron Takuma Dan and Junnosuke Inouye by the Blood Brotherhood League (Ketsumeidan) led by Buddhist priest Nissho Inouye. Police inquiries uncovered seven assassination cells supplied with firearms by naval and army officers, including the late Lieutenant Commander Fujii, and linked suspects to ultra-nationalist patron Mitsuru Toyama and theorist Seikyo Gondo. The report describes Diet debates on rising fascism and social chaos, noting Prime Minister Inukai's admission of underground fascist movements, and includes an enclosure detailing the eighteen indicted assassins and their intended political and financial targets.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 561 from Tokyo on Reactionism, the Blood Brotherhood Assassination League, and Fascist Currents
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Internal State Department summary analyzing a consular report on hidden economic anxiety and moderate diplomatic sentiment in Kyushu.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Memo on Nagasaki reporting: patriotic celebrations masked Kyushu anxiety over Manchurian coal competition; a Fukuoka editorial argued Japan must balance 'Come Back to Asia' sentiment with considerate foreign relations.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Current Thought in Kyushu and Regional Discontent

subfiles.about: Consular report transmitting and analyzing a Fukuoka newspaper editorial advocating diplomatic moderation over extreme Asiatic isolationism.
subfiles.from: Henry B. Hitchcock, American Consul at Nagasaki
subfiles.summary: Consul Hitchcock transmits an editorial from the respected Fukuoka Nichi Nichi Shinbun of March 28, 1932, observing that beneath the surface chauvinism stimulated by returning troops, a silent section of public opinion in Kyushu was uneasy about Manchurian competition and military domination. The translated editorial analyzes the popular slogan 'Come Back to Asia' (an Asiatic Monroe Doctrine), rejecting extreme demands for withdrawal from the League of Nations and warning that diplomacy cannot be played like solitaire. It cautions that insisting entirely on Japan's self-interest while disregarding foreign interests would ultimately isolate the nation.
subfiles.title: Report from Nagasaki Consulate Transmitting Editorial on the Slogan 'Come Back to Asia'
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Despatch No. 560 on Diet debates concerning the capital's atmosphere of terror and right-wing extremism.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Neville's 1932 despatch on Diet interpellations over a 'reign of terror' fostered by misguided patriotism.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.00/384 regarding 'Reign of Terror' in Tokyo and Diet Interpellations

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum evaluating Embassy reporting on the scope, ideology, and danger of extreme nationalist organizations in Japan.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State (W.R.L.)
subfiles.summary: Memo praises Salisbury's compilation of 124 reactionary societies, tracing their 1888 origins and unification behind continental expansion after the Manchurian Incident, warning of a military-subservient cabinet or dictatorship backed by mass patriotic organizations.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum Analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 588 on the Reactionary Movement in Japan

subfiles.about: Major analytical despatch examining the history, ideology, membership, and potential political impact of reactionary and fascist organizations across Japan.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Drafted by Laurence E. Salisbury, this comprehensive despatch analyzes the modern Japanese reactionary movement from its late nineteenth-century origins under figures like Mitsuru Toyama and Ryohei Uchida to its resurgence after the London Naval Treaty and the Manchurian Incident. It evaluates the likelihood of a super-party military-dominated cabinet or military coup, details the split of the proletarian Social Democratic Party (Shakai Minshuto) over state socialism, and examines allied mass groups including the 3,000,000-strong Imperial Reservists Association. Enclosure 1 provides an extensive annotated catalogue of reactionary societies, documenting their founding dates, leadership, publications, and memberships (numbered 1 through 55 in this segment).
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 588 from Tokyo on Reactionary Organizations in Japan, with Annotated Roster of Patriotic Societies
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
